la:adv:denique.html:
dēnĭque, adv.
etym. dub.; perh. dēnĭ, locative of de, and que
.
Orig. denoting succession in time, and thereupon, and then, in the sequel.
In gen. (rare—for syn. cf.: tum, demum, tandem, postremo): omnes negabant ... denique hercle jam pudebat,: risu omnes qui aderant emoriri. Denique Metuebant omnes jam me,: ille imperat reliquis civitatibus obsides. Denique ei rei constituit diem,: ferme ut quisque rem accurat suam, sic ei procedunt post principia denique,.—In the interrogatory formula: quid denique agitis?and what did you do then?: .—More freq.,
Pregn., ending a period, at last, at length; lastly, finally: boat caelum fremitu virum ... Denique, ut voluimus, nostra superat manus,; cf. ; : nisi quia lubet experiri, quo evasuru 'st denique,; cf. ; : Nil nostri miserere? mori me denique coges,: quid jam misero mihi denique restat?; —
Strengthened by ad extremum, ad postremum, or tandem: boni nescio quomodo tardiores sunt, et principiis rerum neglectis ad extremum ipsa denique necessitate excitantur,: victus denique ad postremum est,; fin.: et tandem denique devorato pudore ad Milonem aio, Ap. M. 2, p. 121.—
Sometimes of that which happens after a long delay = tandem: quae (sc. urbana) ego diu ignorans, ex tuis jucundissimis litteris a. d. V. Cal. Jan. denique cognovi,: aliquam mihi partem hodie operae des denique, jam tandem ades ilico,.—
With the particles tum, nunc, or an abl. of time (nearly = demum), just. precisely: tum denique homines nostra intellegimus bona, cum, etc.,: qui convenit polliceri operam suam reip. tum denique, si necessitate cogentur? etc.,; so tum denique,; ; ; et saep.; and separated,; : tantum accessit, ut mihi nunc denique amare videar, antea dilexisse,; cf. : ne is, de cujus officio nemo umquam dubitavit, sexagesimo denique anno dedecore notetur,; cf. ; ; .—
Like demum with pronouns, to give emphasis: si qua metu dempto casta est, ea denique casta est,: is enim denique honos mihi videri solet, qui, etc.,; cf.: eo denique,.—
With vix (like vix demum): posita vix denique mensa,.—
Transf., in enumerations.
Like dein (deinde) followed by postremo, or ad postremum (rare): denique sequitur ... postremo si est, etc.,: omnes urbes, agri, regna denique, postremo etiam vectigalia vestra venierint,; ; ; cf. : primum illis cum Lucanis bellum fuit .. Denique Alexander rex Epiri .. cum omnibus copiis ab his deletus est .. ad postremum Agathocles, etc.,. —
Pregn., to introduce the last of a series, finally, lastly, in fine (the usual meaning of the word; cf.: postremo, novissime, ad extremum): consilium ceperunt ... ut nomen hujus de parricidio deferrent, ut ad eam rem aliquem accusatorem veterem compararent ... denique ut, etc.,; cf. ; : cur etiam secundo proelio aliquos ex suis amitteret? cur vulnerari pateretur optime de se meritos milites?

cur denique fortunam periclitaretur? : aut denique,: qui denique,: tum denique, et saep.: cum de moribus, de virtutibus, denique de republica disputet (Socrates),: mathematici, poetae, musici, medici denique, etc.,: denique etiam,: primum omnium me ipsum vigilare, etc.: deinde magnos animos esse in bonis viris ..: deos denique immortales. auxilium esse laturos,.—

Freq. in ascending to a climax, or to a higher or more general expression, in a word, in fine, in short, briefly, even, in fact, indeed: quis hunc hominem rite dixerit, qui sibi cum suis civibus, qui denique cum omni hominum genere nullam esse juris communionem velit?: nemo bonus, nemo denique civis est, qui, etc.,; ; ; : pernegabo atque obdurabo, perjurabo denique,; cf. ; ; ; : numquam tam mane egredior, neque tam vesperi domum revortor, quin te in fundo conspicer fodere, aut arare, aut aliquid facere denique, Heaut. 1, 1, 15: quod malum majus, seu tantum denique?; : ne nummi pereant, aut pyga aut denique fama,: haec denique ejus fuit postrema oratio,; so ; ; ; ; ; —Hence, freq. emphatic with ipse: arma, tela, locos, tempora, denique naturam ipsam industria vicerat,: hoc denique ipso die,.—With omnia, prius flamma, prius denique omnia, quam, etc., ; ; ; cf.: quidquid denique,.—
In post-Aug. prose (esp. in the jurists), to denote an inference, in consequence, therefore, accordingly: hujus victoriae callide dissimulata laetitia est: denique non solita sacra Philippus illa die fecit, etc.,: pulcherrima Campaniae plaga est: nihil mollius caelo: denique bis floribus vernat,; ; et saep. So in citing a decision for a position assumed: denique Scaevola ait, etc.,; ; : exstat quidem exemplum ejus, qui gessit (sc. magistratum) caecus: Appius denique Claudius caecus consiliis publicis intererat, and 6; 48, 5, 8.—In class. usage denique includes the connective -que; once in Plaut. and often in late Lat. a copul. conj. precedes it: atque hoc denique,: aurum, argentum, et denique aliae res,; . See Hand Turs. II. p. 260-278.

la:adj:densus.html:
densus, a, um, adj.
kindred with δασύς, δαυλός (i. e. δασυλός); cf. Lat. dumus, old form dusmus, and dumetum
,
thick, dense, i. e. consisting of parts crowded together. opp. to rarus (on the contrary, crassus, thick, is opp. to thin, fluid; and spissus, close, compact, with the predominant idea of impenetrability; cf. also: angustus, artus, solidus—class. and freq., esp. in poets and historians; in Cic. very rare).
Lit.
In space: ne dum variantia rerum Tanta queat densis rarisque ex ignibus esse,; cf. (for which densatus et laxatus aër, ); and: (terra) Rara sit an supra morem si densa requiras ... Densa magis Cereri, rarissima quaeque Lyaeo,: densa et glutinosa terra, Col. praef. § 24: silva, poëta ap. ; cf.: densiores silvae,: densissimae silvae,: lucus densissimae opacitatis,: denso corpore nubes,; cf.: denso agmine,; so, agmen (sc. navium),: densum umeris vulgus, et saep.: tunicae,: zmaragdi,: litus,sandy,; cf. : aequor,i. e. frozen.: aër,; cf. caelum,; : nimbi,: caligo,; cf.: densissima nox,pitch-dark night,: umbra, Catull. 65, 13; et saep.— Without distinction, corresp. with crassus,—
Poet. with abl., thickly set with, covered with, full of: loca silvestribus sepibus densa, poëta ap. ; cf.: specus virgis ac vimine,: vallis piceis et acuta cupressu,: Thybris verticibus,: ficus pomis,: corpora setis,; cf. : femina crinibus emptis,: funale lampadibus,: trames

caligine opaca (coupled with obscurus), et saep.—

Transf., of the parts themselves which are crowded together, thick, close, set close: superiorem partem collis densissimis castris (sc. trinis) compleverant,pitched very near together,: sepes,: frutices,: ilex, et saep.: hostes,: ministri,: densior suboles,: dens (pectinis),: comae,; cf. pilae, et saep.— Poet.: densorum turba malorum,.—
In time, of things which take place in close succession, thick, frequent, continuous (mostly poet.): ictus,; cf. plagae,: Aquilo,strong, powerful,: silentia,deep, profound,: amores,: pericula,: usus,: ictus,. —
Trop. of speech, condensed, concise: vox atrox in ira, et aspera ac densa,coarse,: tanta vis in eo (sc. Demosthene) tam densa omnia, etc.,; cf. transf. to the writer himself: densior ille (sc. Demosthenes), hic (sc. Cicero) copiosior, ib. § 106: densus et brevis et semper instans sibi Thucydides, ib. § 73: (Euripides) sententiis densus, ib. § 68.— Adv.: densē (very rare).
In space, thickly, closely, close together: caesae alni,: calcatum quam densissime,: milites densius se commovebant,.—
(Acc. to no. I. B. 2.) In time, frequently, rapidly, one after the other: quod in perpetuitate dicendi eluceat aliquando, idem apud alios densius, apud alios fortasse rarius,: nulla tamen subeunt mihi tempora densius istis,: replicatis quaestionibus dense,

la:verb:denuntio.html:
dē-nuntĭo (-cĭo), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. Orig. t. t. in the lang. of pub. law, relig., and jurispr.,
to give an official intimation, to make an official announcement or declaration of one's intentions (by means of a messenger, herald, etc.); to announce, intimate, declare, = nuntiando declarare; and with a foll. ut or merely the subjunctive, to intimate, order, command (for syn. cf.: edico, indico, narro, nuntio, refero, defero, renuntio, enuntio, dico).
Prop.
Polit. lang.
With acc.: ut omne bellum, quod denuntiatum indictumque non esset, id injustum esse atque impium judicaretur,; so with indictum,fin. (Fragm. ap. ); ; cf.: quos senatus ad denuntiandum bellum miserat,: utrum paucorum ea denuntiata an universae civitatis essent,—
With acc. and inf.: quod sibi Caesar denuntiaret, se Aeduorum injurias non neglecturum, etc.,: cum se scire quae fierent denuntiaret,; et saep. —And with inf. alone: denuntiat centurionibus exsequi caedem,.—
With ut or ne: Gaditanos denuntiavisse Gallonio, ut sua sponte excederet Gadibus; si id non fecisset, sibi consilium capturos,; cf. : nationibus denuntiare, uti auxilia mittant,; cf.: per vicos urbesque, ut commeatus expedirent,: simul denuntiavit ut essent animi parati,: cf.: dictator magistro equitum denuntiavit, ut sese loco teneret, neu, etc.,; and so with ne, ; .—
With simp. subj.: (legati) denuntient Gallicis populis, multitudinem suam domi contineant,; cf. : (Alcibiades) denuntiavit his (militibus), qui in stationibus erant, observarent lumen, etc.,—
In relig. lang.
With acc.: quibus portentis magna populo Romano bella denuntiabantur,: caedem Caesari evidentibus prodigiis,; cf. ; ; —
With ut: si quid tale acciderit, ut a deo denuntiatum videatur, ut exeamus e vita,.—
In jurid. lang.
Alicui testimonium, to summon a witness: si accusator voluerit testimonium eis denuntiare, (cf.: denuntiatio testimonii,); so, testibus: quoniam duo genera sunt testium, aut voluntariorum aut eorum, quibus in judiciis publicis lege denuntiatur,; cf. ib. § 15; .—Absol.: non denuntiavi,.—
To give notice of a suit or process, : de isto fundo, , 32, 95: in foro denuntiat fundum illum suum esse,.—
Litem denuntiare, to summon for immediate trial (late Lat.), ; .—
Transf. beyond the technical sphere, to announce, intimate, declare; to denounce, menace, threaten; with ut, or merely the subjunct., to intimate, order, command. —
Of personal subjects.
With acc.: ille inimicitias mihi denuntiavit,; cf.: populo Romano servitutem,: proscriptionem, caedem, direptionem,; cf. fin.; et saep.: oculis et aspectu vim tribuniciam,; .—
With acc. and inf.: Sex. Alfenus denuntiat, sese procuratorem esse,; cf. (with testificor and ante praedico): cum se ad omnia, de quibus quisque audire vellet esse paratum denuntiaret,; et saep.—
With a relative clause: denuntiasti homo adulescens, quid de summa reipublicae sentires,.—
With ut: mihi Lupus noster subito denuntiavit, ut ad to

scriberem, .—(ε) With simple subjunctive, = moneo, praedico, ante denuntio, abstineant, etc., —(ζ) With de: de isto fundo,—(η) Absol.: monente et denuntiante te,; . —

Of subjects not personal, to give notice, make known, signify, indicate: terra continens adventus hostium multis indiciis ante denuntiat,: illa arma non periculum nobis sed praesidium denuntiant,: si ante exortum nubes globabuntur, hiemem asperam denuntiabunt, etc.,: caeruleus (color) pluviam denuntiat, igneus euros,: hoc juncti boves, hoc paratus equus, hoc data arma denuntiant,: arbor statim pestem denuntians,.

la:adj:denarius.gloss: containing or consisting of ten things
senses: containing or consisting of ten things
la:adj:denarius.html:
dēnārĭus, a, um, adj.
deni
,
containing ten.
In gen.: numerus digitorum,: fistula,ten inches in circumference,; : DENARIAE caerimoniae dicebantur et TRICENARIAE, quibus sacra adituris decem continuis rebus vel triginta certis quibusdam rebus carendum erat, Paul. ex .— Freq.,
Esp. nummus, or absol., de-narius, ii, m. (gen. plur., denarium, ; ; cf. Müll.: denariorum,; ).
A Roman silver coin, which originally contained ten, and afterwards eighteen asses, in value equivalent to an Attic drachma, or about sixteen American cents, Müll.; ; ; Paul. ex Müll.: denarii nummi,: denarii trecenti, 2, 2, 55; so subst., sq.; * ; ; et saep.—
As, an apothecary's weight, = drachma, ; ; et saep.—
A gold coin of the value of 25 silver denarii, ; ; cf. .—
In later times, a copper coin, ; —
Meton. for money in gen., ;

senses: denarius (due to a single coin's value of 10 asses, each made of silver.)

la:verb:denego.gloss: to deny, reject or refuse (a request); to say no
senses: to deny, reject or refuse (a request); to say no
la:verb:denego.html:
dē-nĕgo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
To deny a thing, to say it is not so (very rare): datum denegant, quod datum est,: objecta,.—Far more freq. and class. (cf., on the contrary, abnego).—
To reject, refuse, deny a request, entreaty, etc. (for syn. cf.: nego, infitias eo, infitior, diffiteor, recuso, abnuo, renuo, detrecto).
With acc.: si tibi denegem, quod me oras,: cum id quod antea petenti denegasset, ultro polliceretur,; cf. : auxilia,: praemium dignitatis, quod populus Romanus, cum hujus majoribus semper detulisset, huic denegaret,; ; cf. : sperata gaudia Nymphae Denegat, et saep.; with ellipsis of object: duo rogavi te: ne deneges mihi,.—Poet. of subjects not personal: undas amnis, afflatus ventus,: oratorium ingenium alicui,.—
With inf. or acc. and inf. (poet.): denegavit, se dare granum tritici,; ; (3, 19, 12 M.): dare denegaris,; .—
Absol., ; ; ; ; ; —
With se, to deny one's self, i. e. subject his own will to another's (eccl. Lat.), .

la:noun:denuntiatio.html:
dēnuntĭātĭo (-ciatio), ōnis, f.
denuntio
,
an indication, intimation, announcement, declaration.
With gen. obj. = significatio: quae est enim ista a deis profecta significatio et quasi denuntiatio calamitatum?: belli,; cf. : armorum,: testimonii,threatening to summon as a witness,; cf. denuntio, no. I.: denuntiatione periculi permovere aliquem, by a menacing, *: ingentis terroris,: accusatorum, i. e. information, an informing, = delatio, .—With gen. subj.: Catilinae,: boni civis (i. e. professio, promissio), Planc. ap. : quietis,warning in a dream,.—
Absol.: huic denuntiationi ille pareat? ;

la:verb:denso.html:
denso, āvi, ātum, 1, and (less freq.) denseo, no
perf., ētum, 2 (cf. P.; ib. The MSS. often confound the two forms; densare appears to be critically certain in Liv. and Quint.; densere act. only denset, ; imp. densete, : densebant,: denserent,; also active forms, Apul. Mund. p. 61, 13; ; ; gerund, densendo,; pass. inf. parag. denserier, ; : densetur,: densentur,; , and other forms in Verg.; cf. Wagner,.—See also addenso and condenso), v. a., to make thick, to press together, thicken (not in Cic. and Caes.).
Lit.: Juppiter uvidus austris Densat, erant quae rara modo, et, quae densa, relaxat, (paraphrased: densatus et laxatus aer,); cf.: rarum pectine denset opus,; : ignem,; : omnia,: agmina,; cf. catervas,: ordines,: scutis super capita densatis,: funera, * : glomerata corpus in unum densatur,; cf.: (nubes) largos in imbres,; : obtenta densantur nocte tenebrae,; cf. : hastilia,i. e. hurls thickly,; cf. ictus,: super acervum petrarum radices ejus densabuntur,.—Absol.: (aestus) quasi densendo subtexit caerula nimbis,.—
Trop. of speech, to condense: instandum quibusdam in partibus et densanda oratio,: figuras,.

senses: a tooth, point, spike, prong, tine, fluke, or any tooth-like projection
tooth of envy, envy, ill will
la:noun:dens.html:
dens, dentis (
gen. plur. usually dentium, but dentum is approved by ), m.
root in Sanscr. dantas, Gr. ὀδούς, Goth. tunthus, Germ. Zahn, and Engl. tooth; cf. edo, Engl. eat
, a tooth.
Prop.: cui auro dentes juncti escunt, XII. Tab. 10, 9; ; ; ; : primores,the front teeth,; also called adversi acuti,: praecisores,; and in beasts: rapaces,: canini,the canine teeth, eye-teeth,; ; ; in horses: columellares,; : maxillares,the jaw-teeth, grinders,; called also genuini, Cic. l. l.; and molares, Isid. l. l. et saep.: dentes scalpere,: fricare,: scariphare,; cf. : mobiles confirmare,; cf.: mobiles stabilire,: eximere,to extract,; so, evellere,: extrahere,: excutere, et saep.: dens Indus,i. e. the elephant's,; hence for ivory, ; also called dens Libycus, (3, 29, 12 M.): Numida,; and Erythraeus,.—
Prov.
Albis dentibus deridere aliquem, i. e. to laugh heartily at a person (so as to show one's teeth), .—
Venire sub dentem, to fall into the jaws, under the clutches of, .—
Dentem pro dente, tooth for tooth, .—
Meton. of things resembling a tooth, a tooth, point, spike, prong, tine, fluke, etc.: aratri,; ; cf. Müll.: (irpicis) acc. to : pectinis,; : (clavi) : serrae,; ; cf. , and 6, 58; hence, in architecture, the walls indentated like the teeth of a saw, which connected the two main walls,: forcipis,: (ancorae) ; for falx (vinitorum),the pruning-hook, et saep.—
Trop., the tooth of envy, envy, ill-will: more hominum invident, in conviviis rodunt, in circulis vellicant: non illo inimico sed hoc maledico dente carpunt,: invidus,: ater,.—
Of a destroying power: leti sub dentibus ipsis,; cf. of time: vitiataque dentibus aevi consumere omnia,; and of water: aqua dentes habet,; of malice: malignitatis dentes vitare,, extr. 2.

la:verb:denotatus.html:
dēnŏtātus, ūs, m.
id.
,
a marking or pointing out; only denotatui,

senses: a second time, once again, once more, again
anything which is repeated, once more, again
again, where an action is reversed
la:adv:denuo.html:
dēnŭō, adv.
contr. from dē nŏvo, which never occurs; v. Ruhnk. ; Oud. .; cf.: Fr. de nouveau
,
anew, afresh, again (most freq. in Plaut. and Ter.; elsewh. rare; not in Caes. or the Aug. poets—for syn. cf.: iterum, rursus, ab integro).
Of the restoration of a thing which has been destroyed, = de integro, anew, afresh, ἐκ καινῆς: aedificantur aedes totae denuo,; cf.: urbes terrae motu subversas denuo condidit,: oportet vos nasci denuo,. —
For iterum, a second time, once more, again: si parum intellexti, dicam denuo,; cf. ; : jam ego tibi Persam adducam denuo,: in Etruria rebellante denuo,: denuo in voluntarium exsilium proficiscitur, —
For rursus, of any thing that is repeated (not precisely a second time), once more, again; hence often with verbs compounded with re: ecce Apollo denuo, etc.,: So. Amphitruonis ego sum servus Sosia. Me. Etiam denuo? what, again? ; ; : Sicilia censa denuo est,: recita denuo,.—Pleonast. with redire, ; cf. ; with redauspicari,; with respondere,; with referre, id. Hec. prol. alt. 30. And sometimes with rursus (rursum),; . —
Like our again (in, I am going back again), Gr. αὖ, where an action is reversed (mostly colloquial): aperi ... continuo operito denuo,and then cover it up again,; cf. ; : et nunc quid exspectat, Syre? an dum hinc denuo abeat, etc.,: fiet tibi puniceum corium postea atrum denuo,and then again back,: chlamydem sumam denuo,; ; cf. Hand Turs. II. p. 278-280.

la:verb:denoto.html:
dē-nŏto, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
Lit., to mark, set a mark on, with chalk, color, etc.: pedes venalium creta,: lineam conspicuo colore,.—
Transf.
To mark out, point out, specify, indicate, denote, designate (rare but class.—cf. demonstro): qui uno nuntio atque una significatione litterarum civis Romanos necandos trucidandosque denotavit,: haud dubie Icilios denotante senatu,.—
To take note of, mark with the mind, observe accurately, denotantibus vobis ora ac metum singulorum, : cum denotandis hominum palloribus sufficeret vultus,: quot et quales sint nati,: cum ei res similes occurrant, quas non habeat denotatas,; cf. .—
Trop., to stigmatize, scandalize, brand with reproach or infamy: mollem et effeminatum omni probro,: turpia legata, quae denotandi legatarii gratia scribuntur,: qui gaudet iniquitate denotabitur,—Hence, P. a., dēnŏtātus, marked out, conspicuous.—Comp.: denotatior ad contumeliae morsum,.

la:verb:denudo.html:
dē-nūdo, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. a., to lay bare, make naked, denude.
i. q., nudo, to uncover (rare but class.).
Lit.: denudatis ossibus, Enn. ap. : ne Verres denudetur a pectore, ne cicatrices populus Romanus aspiciat,: capita cum superciliis denudanda tonsori praebuimus,: matresfamilias et adultas aetate virgines,: (surculi) medullam,: femur virginis,.—
Trop., to disclose, reveal, detect, betray, expose: denudavit mihi suum consilium,; cf. : multa incidunt quae invitos denudent,: arcana amici,.—
i. q., spolio, to strip, plunder. *
Lit.: civibus Romanis crudelissime denudatis ac divenditis, Lentul. ap. .— *
Trop.: ne dum novo et alieno ornatu velis ornare juris civilis scientiam, suo quoque eam concesso et tradito spolies atque denudes,.
